scenes.title: Topics & Partitions
scenes.subtitle: How Kafka organizes and scales its data
scenes.narration: Topics and partitions are the two structures Kafka uses to organize events and to spread them for parallel processing.

scenes.title: Topics and Partitions Defined
bullets: A topic is a named category of events
Each topic is split into one or more partitions
A partition is an ordered, append-only log
Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition
scenes.narration: A topic is a named category of events, like orders or clicks. Each topic is split into one or more partitions to allow parallelism. Every partition is an ordered, append-only log where new events get the next position. Crucially, Kafka only guarantees ordering within a single partition, not across the whole topic.

scenes.title: How a Message Lands in a Partition
scenes.narration: When a producer sends an event, Kafka decides which partition it belongs to. If the event has a key, Kafka hashes that key to pick a partition deterministically. If there is no key, events are distributed round-robin. The event is then appended to the end of that partition's log.

scenes.title: Creating a Topic
scenes.code:
# Create a topic with 6 partitions
kafka-topics.sh --create \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders \
  --partitions 6 \
  --replication-factor 3

# Inspect it
kafka-topics.sh --describe \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders
scenes.narration: This command creates an orders topic with six partitions, which sets the maximum parallelism for consumers. The replication factor of three means each partition has three copies for fault tolerance. The describe command then shows the partition layout and which broker leads each one. Choose partition counts carefully, because increasing them later can disrupt key-based ordering.

scenes.text: More partitions mean more parallelism, but also more overhead. Size partition count to your expected consumer throughput, and remember ordering holds only inside a partition.
scenes.narration: As a rule of thumb, more partitions mean more parallelism but also more overhead. Size your partition count to your expected consumer throughput, and always remember that ordering holds only inside a single partition.
